source.title: Polysemanticity or Polysemy? Lexical Identity Confounds Superposition Metrics

page_placements.theme: SAE latents become polysemantic through absorption, hedging and co-occurrence

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how much observed neuron overlap across polysemous-word contexts is attributable to shared word form rather than shared meaning, and argues that standard polysemanticity metrics can misattribute lexical identity to superposition. This refines the interpretation of the claim with new results, rather than reproducing the original vision-model method.
record.gate_note: The study tests language-model MLP activations using polysemous words, synonyms, and unrelated-word pairs; it does not test InceptionV1 or image inputs. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. The study also reports experiments on attention outputs, but the principal neuron-level results below are the MLP analyses.
record.test_reason: A 2×2 factorial decomposition of MLP-neuron overlap in nine transformers shows shared word form drives more overlap than shared meaning. The authors argue that standard polysemanticity metrics count lexical-form detectors as polysemantic and propose a lexically adjusted score. This bears on V6 (apparent mixtures that are really one shared feature, here word form) and V7 (polysemantic status depends on how it is scored). It does not manipulate capacity (V3) or estimate the share of polysemantic neurons (V2).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that a substantial portion of what current metrics call polysemanticity is lexical identity, not superposition: sharing a word form yields more neuron overlap than sharing a meaning across nine models (110M–70B). They add that the confound carries into SAEs (18–36% of features), sits in a compact removable subspace, and harms editing. Sense-blind neurons should not count as superposition evidence, though genuine superposition is not denied. The 57% figure applies only to polysemous inputs.
record.recipe_differences: The original source concerns visual neurons and circuit interpretation; this study instead uses sense-annotated language data, factorial comparisons of MLP activation overlap, neuron classification, and causal/downstream tests in transformer language models.
record.method_sensitivity: The lexical contribution ratio decreases with depth and differs across model families; the study reports higher early-layer values and varying depth trajectories. Nouns have a larger SL–PS gap than verbs, though both categories show a positive gap. The LIS-removal dose changes the PS–SYN gap; 20 dimensions reduce it and 50 reverse it. For the 70B model, NF4 quantization is used. The paper reports that cosine, Jaccard, and magnitude-divergence analyses have the same condition ordering, while magnitude divergence has a reversed ordering by its definition.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretrained GPT-2 SAEs (32k and 128k) and Pythia-410M SAEs have 18–36% of active features sense-blind for polysemous words. A 4× larger dictionary gives nearly identical ratios. Feature #5132 fires sense-blind for 232 words and on 47.5% of inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features inherit lexical-form blending across word senses, and larger dictionaries do not remove it.

fits_no_version.finding: Projecting out 20 lexical-identity-subspace dimensions (≤1% of dims) shrinks the PS–SYN gap by 37–51%, and 50 dimensions reverse it, in GPT-2 and Pythia-1B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The lexical-form contribution to neuron overlap lies in a compact, removable subspace.

fits_no_version.finding: Restricting WSD classifiers and ROME edits to sense-selective neurons improves accuracy (89.8% vs 83.6% for sense-blind) and edit selectivity (0.540 vs 0.519, p=0.002).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Filtering out sense-blind neurons improves downstream sense-targeted tasks.

record.problems: The study uses selected polysemous words and sentence sets, so it does not establish a general rate of polysemantic neurons across all language-model inputs. The authors state that the ≈57% shared-word-form figure applies only to polysemous inputs, and that correction using sense labels is currently limited to controlled evaluations. Ablation effects on perplexity are small (<3 ppl points), and the 70B result is from an NF4-quantized model. The paper reports bootstrap confidence intervals, but many individual table entries do not state uncertainty separately.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports Jaccard and magnitude-divergence condition analyses, attention-output decompositions, additional model/layer Rlex values, per-word ablation results, and supplementary corpus analyses. These are not separately enumerated here to keep the record focused on the principal neuron-overlap, lexical-identity, and causal results; the relevant findings are summarized in gate_note and method_sensitivity.

untested.parts: No estimate of the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, nor of how that share varies by layer. The rows measure lexical-versus-semantic overlap and the sense-selective fraction (<1%) instead.
No manipulation of feature count versus neuron capacity. The authors explicitly do not deny superposition for the remaining overlap.
Initialization, regularization and training noise without capacity pressure.
No manipulation of activation function, architecture or regularization, and no polysemantic-share comparison across families.
Vision neurons and pose-type shared features. Polysemanticity outside polysemous-word inputs.
Which part of the activation range is examined.

missing.what: Lexically adjusted polysemanticity score reclassifies 6.5% (layer 6) to 10.4% (layer-averaged) of flagged GPT-2 neurons; 93–94% of these are confirmed form detectors.
Rlex by layer for BERT, ELECTRA, GPT-2-Med, Pythia-12B and LLaMA-2-13B. BERT minimum 0.209; ELECTRA minimum 0.250 with a rise to 0.542 at layer 11; LLaMA-2-13B falls from 0.91 to 0.25.
CoarseWSD-20 replication: PS>SYN at every layer for GPT-2, BERT and Pythia-1B; GPT-2 Rlex runs from 0.98 (layer 0) to 0.57 (layer 11).
Token-embedding baseline Rlex is 0.71–0.88. MLP layer-0 Rlex exceeds it in autoregressive models but not in BERT or ELECTRA.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V3 'challenges' is dropped. The study does not manipulate capacity and explicitly leaves superposition intact for the remaining overlap; it shows mis-measurement (V6/V7), not a different cause. V2 is untested because no share of polysemantic neurons is estimated. SAE, LIS, WSD and ROME rows are unlinked: they concern SAE features, subspaces or the study's own method. The modest 6.5–10.4% reclassification rate tempers the 'substantial portion' framing. The study is a preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Vision classifiers, InceptionV1, and visual neuron responses.
The study analyzes selected polysemous words and sense-tagged contexts, not a general estimate of the share of all MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts in language models.
It separates lexical identity from semantic overlap, but does not manipulate feature capacity or establish that excess feature count causes the remaining polysemanticity.
Initialization, regularization, and training noise without capacity pressure.

The study compares existing model families, but does not manipulate activation functions, regularization, or architecture to measure changes in the share of polysemantic neurons, and does not test SoLU or modern convnets.
It tests lexical-form explanations for polysemous-word overlap in language models, not the specific visual neurons or whether their mixed visual inputs share a feature such as pose.
It compares overlap metrics and decomposes lexical versus semantic contributions, but does not vary activation-range selection or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.operation_detail: Compared MLP-neuron overlap for same-word/different-sense (PS) and different-word/same-sense (SYN) sentence pairs.

tranche.reason: The paper argues and shows that standard polysemanticity metrics count lexical-form detectors as polysemantic, so superposition-based readings need restating. It also gives its own results on V6 and V7.

source_check.notes: Probes and ablations use SSI-defined sense-blind neurons, not the label-free form detectors (67% overlap). The 57% applies to polysemous inputs only and its model is unnamed (primary results are GPT-2). Table 8 Coll.% is not the ratio of the Active and Blind means shown (32k layer 11: 3.9/18.4 is about 21%, table gives 28.9%), so per-word averaging is presumed. Table 4's BERT minimum (.209, layer 11) disagrees with its caption (0.23 at layer 9).

statements.correction: GPT-2: 67.3% of form detectors are sense-blind (SSI < 0.5) and 0.1% are sense-selective. Sense-blind neuron group: sense probe 41.9% (near chance); form probe ~85%, the same as every group (selective 91.1% sense, random 68.9% sense). Ablating sense-blind neurons lowers sense accuracy by <1 pp (clean 73%). Ordering SL > PS > SYN > CL; PS > SYN in all nine models (Wilcoxon p < 0.001, Holm-Bonferroni). GPT-2 Rlex .735 (L0), .494 (L3), .399 (L10).
statements.problem: Says the label-free form detectors decode form (~85%) but not sense (42%) and that ablating them barely affects sense. The probe and ablation results are for SSI-defined sense-blind neurons, a different group; 67.3% of form detectors fall in that group. All groups, random included, decode form at ~85%. 'Follows word form, not sense' overstates: the study finds that form adds more overlap than sense, not that sense adds none (SYN > CL; Rlex < 1).

statements.correction: GPT-2 Rlex: .735 at layer 0, .399 at layer 10, .290 at layer 11; above zero at every layer. The adjusted score reclassifies 6.5% (layer 6) to 10.4% (layer-averaged) of flagged GPT-2 neurons, 93-94% of them confirmed form detectors. It targets only the top-50 form detectors per word (~1.6% of 3072 neurons); the authors call this a conservative lower bound.
statements.problem: Cites r13 (GPT-2) for late-layer Rlex of 'about 0.25-0.29', but GPT-2's late-layer value is .290. The 0.25 is ELECTRA's minimum at layer 6 (mid-depth; ELECTRA rises to .542 at layer 11) and LLaMA-2-13B at layer 38. The 6.5-10.4% figure comes from correcting only the top-50 form detectors per word, so it does not show that the other flagged neurons are non-lexical.

statements.correction: The adjusted score reclassifies 6.5-10.4% of flagged GPT-2 neurons, 93-94% of them confirmed form detectors; the authors call this a conservative lower bound (top-50 detectors per word). About 57% of the activating pairs of flagged neurons share a word form (polysemous inputs only). The study does not estimate how common unrelated mixtures are.
statements.problem: Uses the 6.5-10.4% reclassification as evidence against 'rare'. That figure is a conservative lower bound, limited to the top-50 form detectors per word, so the remaining flagged neurons were never tested. The authors call flagged neurons predominantly lexical detectors. The cited row r13 (GPT-2 Rlex .290 at layer 11) does not contain this figure.

statements.correction: GPT-2 Rlex: .735 (layer 0), .399 (layer 10), .290 (layer 11). BERT and ELECTRA decline more steeply (ELECTRA minimum .250 at layer 6, then .542 at layer 11). LLaMA-2-13B reaches 0.25 at layer 38. LLaMA-2-70B stays at about 0.35-0.45 across its 80 layers. Rlex CI stays above zero in all models.
statements.problem: Gives 'about 0.25-0.29 in late layers' as a GPT-2 value (r13), but GPT-2's late-layer Rlex is .290. 0.25 is ELECTRA (layer 6, mid-depth) and LLaMA-2-13B (layer 38). The fall with depth is not uniform: ELECTRA rises to .542 at layer 11, and LLaMA-2-70B holds at about 0.35-0.45.
Makes no claim about this study.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Polysemous-word sentence pairs in the tested language models
reader_labels.reason: Same-word/different-sense overlap exceeds different-word/same-sense overlap, so overlap in these settings is not by itself evidence of unrelated semantic features; see r01–r14 and r26–r28. The study does not estimate how many neurons across language models respond to unrelated tokens generally.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Lexical-versus-semantic overlap comparisons in tested transformer MLPs
reader_labels.reason: The measured lexical-only PS condition exceeds the semantic-only SYN condition across nine models, and the paper attributes part of the metric signal to shared word form rather than compression; see r01–r14 and r27.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Interpretation of the remaining overlap and causal mechanism
reader_labels.reason: The study does not manipulate feature capacity or show that superposition is absent; its results isolate a lexical contribution and leave genuine superposition possible, as stated by the authors.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Polysemous-word MLP and SAE features examined in the study
reader_labels.reason: Form detectors and sense-blind features often respond across senses of the same word, encode word identity in probes, and show little sense-accuracy loss when ablated; this supports a lexical-form interpretation for some apparent mixtures, not the specific visual shared-feature examples. See r15–r18, r20–r28, r30, r32, and r34.
